title: Bellarmine allows imputation in a sound sense—ours
source_text: XXXIII. Imo ne quidem nostrum loquendi modum simpliciter damnare audent Scholae Romanae Theologi; concedunt enim sano sensu dici posse justitiam Christi nobis imputari, & fieri nostram. Quin sanus ille sensus juxta quem locutionem istam interpretantur est ille ipse quem nos intendimus. Id manifeste patet ex Bellarmino, lib. 2. de Justif. cap. 7. §. Quarto refellitur. Nam, inquit, si solum vellent haeretici nobis imputari Christi merita, quia nobis donata sunt, & possumus ea Deo Patri offerre pro peccatis nostris, quoniam Christus suscepit super se onus satisfaciendi pro nobis, nosque Deo Patri reconciliandi, recta esset eorum sententia.
pass_a_gloss: Indeed the theologians of the Roman school do not even dare simply to condemn our manner of speaking; for they concede that in a sound sense it can be said that Christ’s righteousness is imputed to us and becomes ours. Nay, that sound sense according to which they interpret that locution is the very one we intend. This is plainly evident from Bellarmine, On Justification book 2, chapter 7, § Quarto refellitur. For, he says, if the heretics only meant that Christ’s merits are imputed to us because they are given to us, and we can offer them to God the Father for our sins, since Christ took on himself the burden of satisfying for us and of reconciling us to God the Father, their opinion would be right.
pass_b_english: Rome concedes a sound sense of imputing Christ’s righteousness—as becoming ours.
Bellarmine: if heretics mean donated merits we may offer the Father, the opinion is right.
